title: FineBooks: are open OCR models good enough to unlock historical knowledge?
gist: Hugging Face and EleutherAI launched FineBooks, benchmarking 14 open-weight VLM-based OCR models against 2,165 expert-transcribed historical book pages; the best (dots.mocr, 3B) hits 97.6% reading accuracy at $1.94 per 1,000 pages, which the authors judge good enough to re-OCR public-domain corpora for LLM training but not yet good enough for scholarly transcription or for libraries dependent on ALTO XML. The stated next step is re-processing roughly 200,000 public-domain items from the Biodiversity Heritage Library's 300,000-item, 64-million-page collection.

themes.theme: OCR quality as the binding constraint on open training data

insights.claim: The Talkie project measured that a language model trained on OCR-derived book text learned at only 30% of the efficiency of the same model trained on human transcriptions of the same books, making transcription quality a first-order determinant of pretraining compute efficiency.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: Data quality, not just data volume, is a lever on training cost — a 3x learning-efficiency penalty means cleaning existing corpora can substitute for buying more compute or scraping more tokens.
insights.quote: a language model trained on OCR-derived text learned at 30% of the efficiency of the same model trained on human transcriptions of the same books
insights.locator: Why do we need better OCR?

insights.claim: Common Pile, described as the largest openly licensed training corpus to date, contains roughly 300,000 public domain books whose text came from earlier, weaker OCR pipelines — meaning a large share of the open-licensed corpus is degraded at the source rather than at the model.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: Existing open corpora are re-processable assets, not fixed inventory; whoever re-OCRs them cheaply captures a quality edge over anyone still training on the legacy text.
insights.locator: Why do we need better OCR?

insights.claim: Re-running modern OCR over already-digitized public domain books is framed as the single highest-leverage available improvement to open-source AI training datasets — a data-refinement play rather than a new-data-acquisition play.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: Signals where marginal open-AI effort is going next: refining owned corpora, which is cheap and uncontested, versus licensing or scraping, which is expensive and litigated.
insights.quote: Re-processing those books with better OCR models is one of the highest-leverage improvements available for open source AI training datasets.
insights.locator: Why do we need better OCR?

insights.claim: Historical books are systematically harder for current OCR models than modern documents because the models were primarily trained on modern documents, while the books carry unusual layouts, archaic letterforms such as the long s (ſ) and ligatures, and dead languages like Latin.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: Benchmark scores on modern-document OCR do not transfer to the archival corpus that holds the untapped open text — domain-shift risk sits between headline model claims and actual dataset value.
insights.locator: Historical books are often considerably more complex

themes.theme: Leaderboard results: size does not buy accuracy

insights.claim: In a 14-model open-weight OCR evaluation on 2,165 historical pages, dots.mocr (3B) led at 97.6% reading accuracy, ahead of OvisOCR2 (0.9B) at 96.9%, PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 (1B) at 96.1%, olmOCR-2 (8.3B) at 95.7%, LightOnOCR-2 (1B) at 95.1%, Qwen3.5-9B (9.7B) at 94.9%, and DeepSeek-OCR (3.3B) at 93.8%.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: A concrete ranking of open OCR weights that any buyer can reproduce for a few dollars — useful for vendor diligence against closed per-page OCR APIs.

insights.claim: Parameter count is inversely related to accuracy across the reported OCR slice: a 0.9B model (OvisOCR2) and a 1B model (PaddleOCR-VL-1.6) both beat an 8.3B model (olmOCR-2) and a 9.7B model (Qwen3.5-9B) on the same 2,165 pages.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: In document-conversion workloads, scale is not the moat — small specialised models undercut large generalist VLMs on both accuracy and inference cost, compressing the pricing power of frontier-model document APIs.

insights.claim: The accuracy leader carries a 4-6x cost premium for under one percentage point of gain: dots.mocr costs $1.94 per 1,000 pages at 97.6% versus $0.46 for OvisOCR2 at 96.9% and $0.34 for PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 at 96.1%.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: At corpus scale the accuracy/cost frontier — not the top of the leaderboard — determines which model gets used, so leaderboard leadership is a weak proxy for deployed share.

insights.claim: Open-weight OCR models can be run entirely without API keys, per-page charges, or restrictions on re-use of the output, removing the recurring-fee structure that commercial document-AI pricing depends on.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: Watch per-page OCR/document-extraction pricing: a free, permissively licensed 97%-accuracy alternative caps what incumbents can charge for commodity page conversion.
insights.quote: Anyone can download these models and run them on their own hardware, without API keys, per-page charges, or restrictions on the re-use of the output.

themes.theme: Evaluation design — the metrics that hide failures

insights.claim: Character Error Rate alone is an unreliable OCR metric because a model can post a good CER while silently dropping content such as footnotes, so recall (share of expected words actually produced) must be scored separately.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: A reusable diligence check for any extraction vendor: ask for recall and omission rates, not just error rate, before trusting a quoted accuracy number.
insights.quote: A model can have a good CER while silently dropping footnotes.

insights.claim: Loop rate — the share of pages where a model repeats itself until it hits its token limit — mechanically inflates a model's other scores because looped pages are excluded from them, so accuracy figures are only interpretable alongside the loop rate.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: A concrete benchmark-gaming vector: any evaluation that drops failed generations before averaging rewards models that fail loudly, which is how published VLM scores get flattered.
insights.quote: Looped pages are excluded from that model's other scores, so a high loop rate makes the remaining numbers look better than they are.

insights.claim: VLM-based OCR models hallucinate text onto blank or illustration-only pages, a failure mode absent from classical OCR pipelines and severe enough that the leaderboard scores over-extraction on those pages as its own category.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: Generative document extraction imports hallucination risk into a task that was previously deterministic — a real reason regulated document workflows may resist the VLM upgrade.
insights.quote: VLM-based models sometimes generate text on blank or illustration-only pages, so the leaderboard scores those pages as a separate category.

insights.claim: The evaluation splits CER into a diplomatic variant (modernising the long-s ſ to s counts as an error) and a reading variant (that modernisation counts as correct), because faithful scholarly transcription and modern readability are different products with different accuracy ceilings.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: Any single quoted OCR accuracy number is definition-dependent; the same model can be 'good enough' or 'not usable' depending on which variant the seller reports.

insights.claim: Open OCR models are judged already good enough for LLM training corpora, because the leading models make far fewer character errors than the legacy pipelines whose output currently populates corpora like Common Pile.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: The re-OCR trade is live now for AI-data builders — no further model progress is required for the corpus-refresh thesis to pay.
insights.locator: Are the open OCR models good enough?

insights.claim: The blocker for libraries replacing legacy OCR is output format, not accuracy: legacy pipelines emit ALTO XML with word-level coordinates that library systems depend on, while the new models emit Markdown or plain text with at most text-region coordinates and never word-level positions.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: Institutional adoption is gated by integration debt rather than model capability — the addressable opportunity is a coordinate-emitting wrapper, not a better model.
insights.quote: The new models output Markdown or plain text, sometimes with text-region coordinates, but never word-level positions, so a library can't simply drop the new text into existing infrastructure built on ALTO XML.
insights.locator: Are they good enough for libraries replacing legacy OCR?

insights.claim: Open OCR models fail scholarly transcription not by misreading pages but by silently normalising archaic features — the long-s (ſ), ligatures and similar — which the author expects focused fine-tuning could largely fix.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: A narrow, cheap fine-tuning gap rather than a capability gap — the remaining unserved segment is likely closed within a model cycle, so don't underwrite a durable moat there.
insights.quote: the gap is not that models misread the page, it is that they silently modernise the long-s (ſ), ligatures, and other text features a scholarly transcription must preserve
insights.locator: Are they good enough for scholarly transcription?

insights.claim: A full 2,165-page evaluation run costs between a few cents and a few dollars per model on per-minute-billed Hugging Face Jobs, with each run pinning the model revision, container image, and script commit so any leaderboard score can be reproduced by re-submitting the same job.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: When benchmarking a model costs single-digit dollars, third-party evaluation stops being a moat and becomes a commodity — bad vendor claims get falsified within days of release.
insights.quote: Billing is per minute. A full 2,165-page run costs between a few cents and a few dollars per model.

insights.claim: Because adding a newly released model costs a single job submission of a few dollars, the leaderboard is designed as a continuously updated tracker of the state of the art rather than a point-in-time snapshot — a response to OCR models arriving several per month.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: Release cadence in open OCR is now fast enough that static benchmarks are obsolete on publication; treat any fixed model comparison older than a month as stale.
insights.quote: the board tracks the state of the art rather than snapshotting it

insights.claim: Expert ground-truth transcriptions produced by the IMPACT project and BHL-Europe in 2011-2012 — 2,165 pages in English, French, German and Latin at roughly one error per two thousand characters — remain the enabling asset fourteen years later, preserved in a GitHub repository under CC-BY after both projects and their websites went offline.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: Human-verified ground truth is the scarce, non-reproducible input in AI evaluation — decade-old labelled data appreciates while the models around it churn.
insights.quote: Fourteen years later, the same 2,165 pages still afford a rigorous evaluation because the work was done carefully and released openly under a CC-BY license.

insights.claim: The Biodiversity Heritage Library was selected as the first FineBooks target partly because it publishes its entire collection as bulk downloads via AWS Open Data, making image-to-transcription matching and full-corpus re-processing operationally feasible.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: Bulk-download availability, not collection size, decides which archives get converted into AI training data — a selection bias worth tracking in what open corpora contain.

themes.theme: Scale of the re-processing pipeline and stated limits

insights.claim: The Biodiversity Heritage Library holds more than 300,000 digitized historical natural history documents and over 64 million pages, of which roughly 200,000 items carry public domain rights statements and are slated for full re-OCR and release as the first FineBooks dataset.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: Sizes the near-term open-data supply increment: a two-thirds-public-domain, 64-million-page scientific corpus entering the open training pool at leaderboard-verified quality.
insights.locator: FineBooks, a new collaboration between Hugging Face and EleutherAI

insights.claim: The leaderboard's ground truth covers only six volumes in four European languages, all printed in antiqua-family typefaces, so the results say nothing about German Fraktur, non-Latin writing systems, non-European languages, or handwriting.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: The 97.6% headline does not generalise to the archives where most non-English heritage text sits — the hard, high-value multilingual and manuscript segments remain unmeasured and unclaimed.
insights.quote: The evaluation therefore says nothing about different typefaces such as German Fraktur, about non-Latin writing systems, non-European languages, or about handwriting.

insights.claim: FineBooks deliberately restricts itself to book-like documents because books are visually uniform — mostly single-column running text with consistent layouts — while newspapers, magazines and archival materials present different failure modes the current leaderboard does not measure.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Majstorovic
insights.so_what: Document-type complexity, not language, is the next capability frontier; multi-column and mixed-layout extraction is where the unresolved technical risk still sits.
